readerTitle: "That's too expensive" is a question, not a verdict
caseNote: 가상 사례 (전기자전거 매장, 사무실 청소 업체, 프로젝트 관리 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: "너무 비싸요"에는 항상 숨은 '무엇에 비해'가 있다. 예산, 다른 대안, 기대한 가치 중 무엇과 비교하는지 먼저 알아내야 맞는 대응을 고를 수 있다.
misconception: 고객이 비싸다고 하면 가격을 깎아 줘야 거래가 성사된다.

sources.text: 영업 실무의 일반 원칙 (가격 이의를 예산, 대안 비교, 가치 인식 문제로 나누어 진단하기)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 자전거 할인: $1,200의 10% = $120. 청소 업체: 월 $2,400, 범위 축소 후 월 $1,700은 가정한 수치입니다.
특정 연구나 통계(예: '가격 이의의 몇 %가 실제로는 가치 문제다')는 인용하지 않았습니다. 이런 수치를 추가하려면 1차 출처를 먼저 확인하세요.

cards.title: "That's too expensive" is a question, not a verdict
body: On the same Monday, two owners hear the same four words. A bike shop owner hears them from a shopper. A cleaning company owner hears them from an office manager.
One cuts the price on the spot. The other asks a question. Only one of them learns why the customer said it.

image.label: Two counters, one sentence: 'That's too expensive'
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 자전거 매장 계산대, 오른쪽은 사무실 회의 테이블. 양쪽 고객 머리 위에 같은 말풍선 "That's too expensive." 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A shopper balks at a $1,200 e-bike.
body: You run a bike shop. A customer test-rides your $1,200 electric bike, smiles, then says: "It's great, but it's too expensive."
What do you say next?

options.text: "I can do 10% off if you buy today."
options.feedback: It might close the sale, but you give away $120 without knowing what the problem was. If the issue was something else, the discount may not even help.

options.text: "Fair enough. Too expensive compared to what?"
options.feedback: You learn what the price is being measured against before you spend anything. The answer tells you which response actually fits.

options.text: "No problem, let me show you our $700 model."
options.feedback: Helpful if the budget is truly fixed. But you may talk them out of the bike they loved, for a reason you guessed instead of heard.

cards.title: Same words, different answers.
body: The bike shop owner offered 10% off. The shopper said thanks and left anyway. Later the owner realized the shopper had mentioned a $600 bike online, and never heard why the $1,200 one was worth more.

The cleaning company owner, quoting $2,400 a month, asked what the office manager was comparing it to. The answer: "Our receptionist tidies up now, and that costs us nothing." Now the owner knew the real conversation. It wasn't about the price. It was about what "nothing" was really costing.

image.label: Two paths: a discount leads to a dead end, a question leads to a conversation
image.brief: 두 갈래 길 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 길 "10% off"는 막다른 벽으로 끝나고, 오른쪽 길 "Compared to what?"은 대화 말풍선 여러 개로 이어짐. 단순한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: A price objection is a hidden comparison.
body: A **price objection** is when a customer pushes back on what you charge. "Too expensive" always has an unspoken ending: *compared to something*.
That something might be their budget, another option, or the value they expect to get. Until you know which one, any answer you give is a guess.
So the first job isn't to defend the price or drop it. It's to find the comparison.

cards.title: Three meanings, three different fixes.
body: "Too expensive" usually means one of these:
list: **Over budget:** they can't pay this much now. Try a smaller version, phased work or payment terms.
**Cheaper alternative:** another product, doing it themselves, or doing nothing. Show what the difference buys them.
**Not worth it yet:** they don't see enough value. Go back to their problem and connect the price to it.
cards.callout: A discount only answers the first one, and only partly.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the hidden comparison is often a spreadsheet or a free tool the team already uses. The real question is what that free option costs in time and mistakes.

cards.title: If you move on price, move something else too.
body: Sometimes the budget really is the limit. The cleaning company owner could drop to $1,700 a month, but not for the same service. Instead, the owner offered three visits a week instead of five.
This keeps your price honest. If the price falls with nothing in return, customers learn that your first number wasn't real. If something changes, the price still means something.
Trade, don't cave.

image.label: A scale: lower price on one side, smaller scope on the other
image.brief: 저울 일러스트. 한쪽 접시에 "$1,700/month", 다른 쪽에 "3 visits a week" 카드가 올라가 균형을 이룸. 차분한 파스텔 톤.

cards.title: Sometimes it really is too expensive.
body: Not every objection can be solved. Some customers simply aren't a fit at your price, and that's fine. Letting them go politely beats a deal that leaves you losing money.
Listen for patterns too. If most people say the same thing about the same product, the problem may be your price or how you explain it, not the customer.
And ask sincerely. "Compared to what?" works as a real question. Used as a trick, it feels like pressure.

cards.title: Now it's a software subscription.
body: You sell project-management software at $49 per user a month. A 10-person design agency loved the trial. On the call, the owner says: "It's too expensive for us."
What's your best next move?

options.text: Drop to $29 per user to win the account
options.feedback: You might win this deal, but you cut your price by 40% without knowing why. The agency may expect the same discount at every renewal.

options.text: Ask what they use now, then match the fix to the answer
options.feedback: If it's budget, fewer seats or annual terms may work. If it's a free tool, you can show what switching saves. You only spend what the real problem needs.

options.text: Send a calculator showing how much time they'll save
options.feedback: Strong if the issue is value. But if they're simply over budget, a bigger savings number won't change what they can pay this month.

cards.title: Find the comparison before you touch the price.
body: "Too expensive" means too expensive compared to a budget, an alternative or the value they expect. Each needs a different answer, and only one sometimes needs a lower price.
**Try it today:** think of the last customer who said your price was too high. Write down what they were really comparing it to.
